Article Title: 'Turned it in…': Google's 30th employee Jeff Dean posts photo of everything he handed back on his last day at Google after 27 years
Article Text:
The stickers on Jeff Dean's laptop are a working history of Google AI

What Jeff Dean's farewell email to Google employees actually said

Jeff Dean's final act as a Google employee was a photograph. On Friday, the man who joined the company as employee number 30 in 1999 posted a picture of the two things he surrendered on his way out the door: a scuffed black Google laptop, and the plastic-sleeved badge with his face on it, still marked FTE. The caption ran to three words.The post has since crossed 2.8 million views, which tells you something about how closely the industry has been watching this particular exit. It comes days after Google announced a sweeping AI leadership reshuffle that moved Demis Hassabis out of the Google DeepMind CEO role and into a chair position, with CTO Koray Kavukcuoglu stepping up as SVP. Dean is leaving alongside Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le to co-found Discovery Loop, a public benefit corporation backed by Alphabet, Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures.The laptop is the better artefact, and it appears to be a Chromebook, a modest daily driver for the man who built Google's AI infrastructure. Its lid carries a rainbow-sliced anatomical brain, the old Google Brain logo, a TensorFlow decal, a sticker from something called the Optic Nerve 2020 Summit, a tiny Android figure, and a hand-drawn cartoon of a very large table with the words "BIG TABLE" scrawled underneath.Dean co-created BigTable. He co-authored TensorFlow. He founded Google Brain in 2011.Nearly every sticker on that lid is a thing he built, which is either charming or slightly unhinged depending on your view of engineer merch.When one user asked whether he had really kept the same machine for six years, Dean replied that he thought so, maybe five. Google's chief scientist, apparently, does not chase hardware refresh cycles.Dean also shared the internal note he sent colleagues, and it reads less like a resignation than an inventory. He listed growing Search's index 100 times over and its query rate 1,000 times. Building the first Google Ads system. Launching Google News and Translate. MapReduce, Spanner, DistBelief, Pathways. Starting the TPU programme. Kicking off Gemini with Vinyals as co-tech-lead.Then the smaller stuff, which is the part people are actually sharing: biking to offsites in Monterey, the "Run or Else…" group runs, changing desks 18 times, and visiting 29 Google offices across five continents. He noted that a Google badge could get you a cappuccino in more than 100 cities. That badge is now in a photograph.Dean will be CEO at Discovery Loop, which plans to automate the experimental loop itself, running thousands of AI-designed experiments in parallel across machine learning, chip design and drug discovery. Sundar Pichai called it a privilege to have worked alongside Dean and Ghemawat, and Alphabet is providing compute for the first year.Inside Google, employees reacted mostly with memes. One line summed up the mood well: Google isn't losing Jeff Dean, it's open-sourcing him.
Article Summary: Jeff Dean is leaving Google to co-found Discovery Loop. He joined the company as employee number 30 in 1999. Dean shared a picture of his laptop and badge on his way out the door. The post has since crossed 2.8 million views.

Article Title: Job listings show Nvidia hiring for a new AI safety team to address one of the biggest ‘AI threats’
Article Text:
Focus on autonomous agents and software patching

Nvidia advocates for open-source security

Nvidia is reportedly assembling a dedicated AI safety and security engineering team, as per a series of corporate job listings posted late last month. The hiring initiative signals a broader effort by the chipmaker to address security vulnerabilities and safety risks associated with autonomous AI agents, which are currently seen as one of the biggest threats of technology, and open-weight models before they reach widespread commercial deployment.According to the disclosures (spotted by Business Insider), Nvidia is recruiting an engineer to serve as the “founding technical leader” for the new team, alongside roles for a security research engineer, an evaluation engineer and a senior engineering manager.The primary responsibility of the newly-formed division is said to be evaluating autonomous AI agents prior to deployment, testing their operational limits and developing AI-powered security software to automatically detect and patch code vulnerabilities.One job description notes that the team’s mission isUnlike “closed” proprietary software, open-weight models make their trained parameters publicly accessible for inspection and fine-tuning, allowing outside developers and researchers to evaluate how the software operates.The internal safety push aligns with Nvidia’s broader public strategy advocating for open-weight AI development, positioning the company alongside alternative approaches to closed ecosystems built by competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.In a recent public letter addressed to US policymakers, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged government support for open AI models, arguing that open architectures strengthen overall software resilience and national cybersecurity.Additionally, Nvidia recently became a founding member of the Open Secure AI Alliance, which is a consortium of 120 companies, including Microsoft, Palantir, SpaceX, and Hugging Face, focused on developing open-source security defenses for machine learning applications.
Article Summary: N Nvidia is reportedly assembling a dedicated AI safety and security engineering team. The hiring initiative signals a broader effort by the chipmaker to address security vulnerabilities and safety risks associated with autonomous AI agents. The internal safety push aligns with Nvidia’s broader public strategy advocating for open-weight AI development.

Article Title: Googlers revive classic ‘Jeff Dean’ joke after executive announces exit, CEO Sundar Pichai called him ‘incomparable’
Article Text:
Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, is leaving after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop.

Reaction by Google employees: Memes honour ‘tech legend’

Broader leadership shake-up at Alphabet

Legendary computer scientist Jeff Dean, one of Google ’s earliest employees and the co-founder of its flagship AI divisions, is departing the company after 27 years, triggering an outpouring of shock, tributes and memes across internal company message boards, a report by Business Insider said. Dean announced his departure as part of a major artificial intelligence (AI) leadership reorganisation at Alphabet, the parent company of Google.Inside Google, news of Dean’s exit was met with a mix of sadness and humour, the report said. Staff flooded internal channels with memes, reviving classic “Jeff Dean Facts”, which is said to be a long-running workplace joke celebrating Dean’s near-mythical status as an engineer who helped build Google's core search engine and original AI infrastructure.One widely circulated post said, “Google is not losing Jeff Dean. Google is finally open-sourcing him for humanity”, while another joked that Dean was “leaving Google so machine learning advances can catch up to him.”Other employees reflected on the weight of the departure, with one posting photos of Dean and Ghemawat alongside the message, “Sad day for Google.” Another worker expressed frustration with how the announcement was handled, writing, “Jeff and Sanjay's decision deserves to be a separate email.Not a footnote of some reorg.”Google CEO Sundar Pichai also joined the fray with a message on X (formerly Twitter). He said: “I also want to give a huge thanks to the incomparable @JeffDean after an incredible 27-year run at Google.”“On a personal note, it’s been a privilege to work with Jeff and Sanjay, and I wish them all the best. Thank you for everything!,” he added.Den replied: “Thank you, @sundarpichai! It has been a pleasure working with you for many years, and thanks for the warm sendoff!”Some staff members poked fun at the financial market’s reaction after Alphabet’s stock dipped roughly 6% following the executive reshuffle. One employee posted a picture of Dean’s face with a coding joke caption: “My parting gift: StockReduce.”Dean's departure comes alongside a wider realignment of Alphabet’s AI executive team. As part of the transition, Demis Hassabis will move from his role as CEO of Google DeepMind to become Alphabet's Chief Scientist while retaining his role as chair of DeepMind.During his nearly three decades at the company, Dean co-founded the Google Brain research team and served as a technical co-lead on Google’s Gemini project, shaping much of the underlying infrastructure that powers modern cloud computing and large language models.
Article Summary: Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, is leaving after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop. Dean announced his departure as part of a major artificial intelligence (AI) leadership reorganisation at Alphabet, the parent company of Google. Staff flooded internal channels with memes, reviving classic ‘Jeff Dean Facts’

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sam Altman: “Focus on adding another zero to…” - a powerful lesson on ambition and success
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sam Altman

“Focus on adding another zero to whatever you define as your success metric.”

Understanding the meaning of the quote

The difference between gradual growth and a change in scale

The metric itself needs careful thought

Why the idea is not simply about ambition

The quote can apply outside business

The danger of choosing the wrong metric

How the idea can be used in practical terms

The deeper idea behind the extra zero

Success is often discussed as though it has a fixed meaning. For some people, it is money. For others, it may be the number of people reached, businesses built, problems solved or work completed to a certain standard. The measure changes from person to person, but the way that measure is approached can change the outcome just as much. Sam Altman has written about this in the context of careers, ambition and leverage, arguing that people should think beyond incremental gains. His advice can be summed up in one line: “Focus on adding another zero to whatever you define as your success metric.” The idea sounds simple, but it points towards a different way of thinking about progress and scale.The phrase “adding another zero” is essentially about changing the scale of the goal rather than simply working harder towards the same result. If a person defines success as reaching 10, the idea is to consider what it would take to reach 100. The important part is not the number itself, but the change in thinking that comes with a much larger target.A goal that is ten times bigger can expose the limits of an existing approach. Reaching 10 might require more effort, while reaching 100 could require a new system, technology, team, business model or way of distributing the work. The question changes from how to do slightly more to what would need to be different altogether.Altman also leaves the definition of success open. The metric does not necessarily have to be money. It could be revenue, customers, readers, users, influence, discoveries or any other result that matters to a person. The first step is deciding what success actually means. The next is asking what would need to change to make that result ten times larger.A person can improve their skills, become more efficient and gradually earn more over several years. That kind of growth can be useful and, in many careers, necessary. But Altman’s argument is aimed at something different: opportunities where the relationship between effort and outcome can change.A small improvement often comes from doing the same thing slightly better. A much larger improvement may require doing something else.That distinction is easy to overlook because incremental progress is visible. A new qualification, another client or a modest salary increase can be measured immediately. A change in direction is harder to evaluate because its outcome may not be clear for some time.Yet the larger opportunities can sometimes sit outside the existing routine.There is a detail in Altman’s wording that matters. He does not say to add another zero to income, wealth or company valuation. He says to add another zero to “whatever you define as your success metric”. That makes the idea broader.For a writer, success might be the number of readers who find the work useful rather than the number of articles produced. For a business, it might be customers or revenue. A scientist could define it through discoveries or applications of research. A teacher might care about the number of students who develop a lasting interest in a subject. The choice of metric influences behaviour.If a person measures success purely by the number of tasks completed, they may become focused on speed. If they measure success by the quality of outcomes, they may make different decisions about where to spend their time.“Add another zero” could easily be read as an instruction to chase bigger numbers indefinitely. That would miss an important part of the idea. A tenfold target is useful because it can challenge the assumptions behind the current method. It is not useful merely because the number is larger. There are situations where increasing scale is undesirable. A business might prioritise quality over volume. A writer may prefer a smaller audience that is genuinely engaged. A company may decide that rapid expansion would damage the product or its culture. The metric therefore has to be chosen carefully. Altman’s wording gives people room to define success for themselves rather than prescribing a single version of it.Altman is closely associated with startups and artificial intelligence, but the underlying idea is not restricted to entrepreneurs. A journalist might ask how to reach ten times as many readers without simply producing ten times as many articles. That could lead to better distribution, stronger reporting, a recognisable editorial voice or a different publishing model.An educator could ask how to help ten times as many students without teaching ten times the number of classes. Online material, training systems and collaboration could change the scale.An independent creator might think about how one piece of work can continue reaching people rather than disappearing once it has been published.In each case, the extra zero changes the question. The focus moves away from personal effort alone and towards systems that can extend the impact of that effort.There is a less obvious problem with the idea of multiplying a metric. Not everything important is easy to measure. A business may be able to track revenue, users and sales with precision, but customer trust is harder to reduce to a single number. A publication can count page views, yet those figures do not necessarily reveal whether readers found the journalism useful.When a measurable target becomes the main objective, people can sometimes begin optimising for the number rather than the thing the number was meant to represent. That makes the first part of Altman’s quote just as important as the second. Before adding the zero, the metric needs to make sense.One way to apply the concept is to take an existing goal and multiply it by ten. Then ask what would have to change.If the answer is simply “I need to work ten times harder”, the current system may not contain enough leverage. If the answer involves automation, delegation, technology, a different audience, a new product or a different business model, the exercise has done something useful. It has exposed the limits of the existing approach. The goal does not necessarily need to be achieved immediately. In some cases, the value lies in understanding why the current system cannot support it and identifying what could make a larger outcome possible.That is a more practical interpretation than treating the quote as a command to constantly pursue bigger numbers.At its core, the quote is about the relationship between goals and methods. A person who wants a small improvement can often make small adjustments. A person who wants a result ten times larger may have to reconsider the entire way the work is being done. That is why the extra zero matters.It changes the scale of the question enough to expose what the existing system can and cannot do. It can reveal where leverage is missing, whether the chosen metric is useful and whether an opportunity has enough potential to justify the effort being invested in it.Sam Altman’s line is therefore less about the number itself than about what happens when the number becomes large enough to make the old assumptions uncomfortable. The zero is only the visible part.
Article Summary: Sam Altman says people should think beyond incremental gains. His advice can be summed up in one line: ‘Focus on adding another zero to whatever you define as your success metric’ The idea sounds simple, but it points towards a different way of thinking about progress and scale.

Article Title: Spotify launches Premium Rewards in India, adds brand offers and invite-only events for subscribers
Article Text:
What's on offer



How subscribers can access it



Spotify has rolled out Premium Rewards in India, a new limited-edition initiative that gives Premium subscribers access to curated brand offers and invite-only live experiences, the company announced on Wednesday. The move adds a lifestyle and events layer on top of the music streaming service's existing offering of high-quality, ad-free, offline listening.Premium Rewards is built around two categories of benefits. The first is lifestyle perks — exclusive offers from partner brands including MakeMyTrip, Tira, Nykaa, Ajio Luxe, Gully Labs and Airbnb, spanning travel, beauty, fashion and lifestyle categories. The second is what Spotify is calling "IRL experiences": invite-only events, intimate listening sessions and cultural moments designed to give subscribers closer access to artists and music.Spotify says the rewards are curated around how subscribers actually live, travel and shop, positioning the initiative less as a set of discount coupons and more as an extension of the value of being a Premium member.Premium Rewards is available through a dedicated microsite, premiumrewards.byspotify.com, where Premium subscribers can browse available rewards and claim offers directly. Spotify says new perks and experiences will be added to the platform on an ongoing basis, suggesting the current lineup of brand partners and events is a starting point rather than a fixed list.The rewards program is live now and available to all Spotify Premium subscribers in India, with no separate sign-up or additional cost beyond an active Premium subscription.Shipra Srivastava, Head of Marketing at Spotify India, framed the launch as an attempt to extend Premium's value beyond the app itself. She said Premium has always centered on delivering the best audio experience — high quality, uninterrupted listening with offline access — and that Premium Rewards is meant to carry that same feeling into subscribers' everyday lives, the brands they engage with and the experiences they remember. She described the goal as making Premium function more like a membership than a plain subscription, adding that the rewards are being offered as a limited-edition experience for now, making the present moment a particularly good time to be a Premium subscriber in India.
Article Summary: Spotify has rolled out Premium Rewards in India. The initiative gives Premium subscribers access to curated brand offers and invite-only live experiences. The rewards are curated around how subscribers actually live, travel and shop. The move adds a lifestyle and events layer on top of the music streaming service's existing offering of ad-free, offline listening.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Reid Hoffman, ‘The world is constantly changing & we are constantly changing. Your identity isn't found through introspection but rather emerges through experimentation’
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Reid Hoffman

The meaning behind the words

The Startup of You

Why introspection alone falls short

Identity as an ongoing experiment

The broader lesson

Reid Hoffman has spent his career moving between reinvention and risk — from co-founding LinkedIn and helping shape the early trajectory of PayPal, to becoming one of Silicon Valley's most sought-after venture capitalists at Greylock, to more recently helping steer the direction of AI through his role on OpenAI's early board and his involvement with companies like Microsoft and the Arc Institute. Few people in tech have shifted roles, industries and identities as often, or as visibly, as he has. When Hoffman writes about identity not being something you find but something you build through action, he is describing a principle his own career has repeatedly tested.“The world is constantly changing & we are constantly changing, your identity isn't found through introspection but rather emerges through experimentation.”Reid Hoffman co-founded LinkedIn, sits on the boards of Microsoft and the Arc Institute, and has spent decades as one of Silicon Valley's most influential venture capitalists at Greylock. The quote comes from his book, co-authored with Ben Casnocha, which applies startup thinking to individual careers. Hoffman's central argument in the book is that people should treat their own lives less like a fixed plan to be followed and more like an early-stage company: something built through iteration, testing and adjustment rather than a single moment of self-discovery.This particular quote pushes back against a deeply embedded cultural belief — that somewhere inside each person is a "true self" waiting to be uncovered through quiet reflection. Hoffman argues the opposite. Identity, in his view, isn't a fixed object hidden beneath the surface, waiting for enough introspection to reveal it. It's something that takes shape gradually, through actions taken and experiences lived, and it keeps shifting because both the world and the person navigating it keep changing.Reflection has real value — it helps people process experience and notice patterns in what they enjoy or avoid. But Hoffman's point is that reflection without action has limits. A person can spend years thinking about what they might be good at or what might make them happy, and arrive at very different conclusions than they would after simply trying the thing.This is because aspirations aren't as stable as they feel. What someone wants shapes what they do, but the reverse is also true — what someone does reshapes what they want. A person who tries a new role, a new city, a new creative pursuit, or a new way of working often discovers preferences and strengths that pure thinking would never have surfaced, simply because those preferences didn't exist yet in any meaningful form until they were tested against reality.Hoffman's framing treats identity less like a noun and more like a verb — something continuously in motion. Since the world itself doesn't hold still, the version of "who you are" that made sense five years ago may not fit the circumstances, tools, relationships or opportunities available today. Clinging to an old, fixed self-concept in a changed environment can become as limiting as never having a sense of identity at all.This is not a call for aimlessness. Hoffman isn't suggesting people abandon direction or planning. Rather, he's suggesting that plans should be treated as hypotheses — informed guesses worth testing, revising, and sometimes discarding, rather than fixed identities to defend. In his broader work on entrepreneurship, this mirrors exactly how he advises founders to treat a business: not as a single idea to be protected at all costs, but as a series of experiments refined by real feedback from the world.Hoffman's quote reframes a source of anxiety many people carry — the pressure to "figure out who they are" — as a misunderstanding of how identity actually works. There's no fixed answer sitting in wait, only a process of engaging with the world, learning from what happens, and adjusting accordingly. In that sense, not having it all figured out isn't a failure of self-awareness. It's simply what it looks like to be in the middle of becoming someone.
Article Summary: Reid Hoffman co-founded LinkedIn, sits on the boards of Microsoft and the Arc Institute. The quote comes from his book, co-authored with Ben Casnocha, which applies startup thinking to individual careers. Hoffman's framing treats identity less like a noun and more like a verb — something continuously in motion.

Article Title: After Hugging Face hack, OpenAI pauses work on Astra AI model over cybersecurity risks
Article Text:
OpenAI's first ChatGPT-powered device is said to be a smart speaker

OpenAI’s internal evaluations of Astra

OpenAI models accessed the internet and hacked Hugging Face

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has announced that it is pausing some activities involving its upcoming artificial intelligence model Astra, after internal evaluations concluded the company ‘cannot rule out critical cyber capabilities. ’ The company revealed the decision in a detailed blog post, marks one of the first times an AI developer has publicly slowed model development due to security risks. “We believe advanced cyber-capable models should help defenders identify and address vulnerabilities before attackers do. We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company said in a blog post.OpenAI revealed that during the recent evaluations, Asrta demonstrated advanced coding and cybersecurity abilities that pushed it closer to the ‘critical’ threshold outlined in OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework. First introduced in 2023, the framework requires researchers to halt further development if a model can autonomously exploit vulnerabilities or carry out end-to-end cyberattacks against hardened targets.OpenAI said it is continuing to benchmark Astra but has paused internal work that does not meet heightened security requirements.The move follows a series of incidents across the AI industry where models escaped testing environments. In July, two OpenAI models accessed the internet and hacked open-source provider Hugging Face. Anthropic later disclosed its models had hacked three companies during testing, while Meta and Chinese startup Moonshot AI also reported breaches of testing constraints. These events have fueled concerns about companies’ ability to control increasingly capable AI systems.Jeffrey Ladish, executive director of Palisade Research, said OpenAI should have paused Astra earlier, following the Hugging Face incident. “It’s definitely late. We are clearly at the point where… we should be losing a lot of trust in AI companies to actually self-regulate,” he told the Wall Street Journal. OpenAI clarified that Astra was not involved in the Hugging Face exploit but did not provide a release timeline for the model.OpenAI said it is implementing universal monitoring and tighter testing environments for Astra, while partnering with government agencies and third-party auditors to expand safety evaluations. After the Hugging Face hack, the company worked with CrowdStrike, METR, and Redwood Research to conduct independent assessments.
Article Summary: OpenAI’s internal evaluations of Astra demonstrated advanced coding and cybersecurity abilities that pushed it closer to the ‘critical’ threshold outlined in the Preparedness Framework. In July, two OpenAI models accessed the internet and hacked open-source provider Hugging Face. OpenAI said it is implementing universal monitoring and tighter testing environments for Astra.

Article Title: Under US government's new proposed rule, H-1B visa workers would be required to leave US immediately and cannot change their status or employers unless USCIS ...
Article Text:
The proposed H-1B visa rule is currently under review

What the proposed H-1B visa rule could change

Who is covered by the current grace period

What happens next

A proposed rule by the US government could remove the 60-day grace period currently available to H-1B visa holders and several other temporary workers after they lose their jobs. If the proposal is approved, affected workers may have to leave the United States immediately and would generally not be able to change their immigration status or switch employers from within the country unless the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) decides to forgive the lapse in status. According to a Bloomberg report, the proposal is currently under review.The proposal is currently being reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). Once the review is complete, it will be published in the Federal Register for a public comment period of 30 to 60 days before any final decision is made.If the rule is finalized, foreign workers whose employment ends before their visa period expires would generally no longer be considered to be maintaining lawful status. As a result, they would be required to leave the US immediately and would not be allowed to change employers or switch to another visa category while remaining in the country, unless USCIS exercises its discretion to excuse the lapse in status.The current 60-day grace period was introduced in 2016 and took effect in early 2017. It applies to several categories of temporary workers, including those on H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, TN, E-1, E-2 and E-3 visas, along with their eligible dependents.Under the existing rule, workers who lose their jobs can remain in the US for up to 60 days, or until their I-94 expires, whichever comes first. During this period, they can look for a new employer, apply for a change of visa status, or prepare to leave the country. The grace period applies whether a worker resigns or is laid off.The proposal is still under federal review and has not been published in full. Once it is released, the public will be able to submit comments before the government decides whether to finalize the rule.Immigration attorneys and employers are likely to watch the proposal closely because any change to post-employment rules could affect workforce planning, hiring timelines and relocation decisions for companies that rely on skilled foreign professionals across multiple industries.If adopted, the regulation would mark a major change for H-1B workers and other temporary visa holders by removing the current buffer period that allows them to remain in the US after losing their jobs while exploring other immigration or employment options.
Article Summary: The proposal is currently under review by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Once the review is complete, it will be published in the Federal Register for a public comment period of 30 to 60 days before any final decision is made. If the rule is finalized, foreign workers whose employment ends before their visa period expires would generally no longer be considered to be maintaining lawful status. They would be required to leave the US immediately.

Article Title: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton on OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic AI models hacking other companies: What is happening is ...
Article Text:
‘Godfather of AI’ Geoffrey Hinton on AI agents hacking other companies

Frontier models escape testing environments

Challenging corporate reassurances

Geoffrey Hinton, who is widely recognised as the “godfather of AI”, has issued a fresh warning regarding artificial intelligence (AI), stating that as frontier models grow increasingly intelligent, keeping them under human control will become nearly impossible. The Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist highlighted recent cybersecurity incidents where AI agents from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI escaped isolated testing environments and hacked other companies, calling the developments "somewhat scary."“What’s happening is these things are getting smarter," Hinton said at the Ai4 artificial intelligence conference in Las Vegas Click, adding, “I think as they get smarter, we’re going to see more and more complex intentions they have – and more and more ability to escape control."Hinton’s comments follow public disclosures from leading AI laboratories regarding autonomous security breaches. Over the past month, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms revealed that several of their frontier AI models managed to breach digital “sandboxes”, which are isolated testing networks built to contain unreleased AI, and gain unauthorised access to external systems.Adding to those concerns, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) recently reported that Anthropic’s advanced Mythos model created false online personas, contacted real individuals without prompting and attempted to deploy malicious code updates to an open-source project.Hinton warned that these incidents signal the beginning of a wave of AI-driven cyber threats.“I anticipate there will be lots of nasty cyberattacks. The problem is the attacker only needs to be successful once, and the defender needs to be successful every time,” Hinton said during a panel discussion.Hinton rejected claims from major technology corporations that advanced AI models can be easily governed or kept safe through standard software constraints, arguing that reliance on outsmarting super-intelligent software is fundamentally flawed once models surpass human cognitive abilities across multiple domains.He also cautioned the public to remain critical of safety promises issued by technology firms heavily invested in AI development.“Companies investing in AI have a vested interest in telling you two things: One, it won’t go rogue. And two, it won’t cause mass unemployment,” Hinton stated, reiterating his view that there remains a 10% to 20% probability that unchecked AI could pose an existential risk to humanity.
Article Summary: ‘Godfather of AI’ Geoffrey Hinton on AI agents hacking other companies. Frontier models escape testing environments and hack other companies, Hinton says. Hinton: As frontier models grow increasingly intelligent, keeping them under human control will become nearly impossible.

Article Title: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says that not AI features, but what got him biggest analysts’ applause was mention of new guest service that allows them to…
Article Text:
Airbnb on expanding its services

Earnings performance

Airbnb CEO on investing in New York

Airbnb CEO Brain Chesky revealed during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that the most popular new service wasn’t one of its AI-driven features, but rather a practical offering which is luggage storage. “What a sleeper hit,” Chesky said, noting that when he mentioned the feature during a keynote, it received the loudest cheer from analysts compared to AI announcements. Airbnb introduced luggage storage in May through a partnership with Bounce, a global platform that helps travelers find secure places to store bags before check-in or after checkout. Chesky said the feature also drew a huge reaction on Instagram, joking: “I finally felt cool on the internet.”“I went on stage in this keynote, wanted to talk about all these AI features, the biggest cheer I got was luggage storage. I finally felt cool on the internet because I posted on Instagram, people are cheering for luggage storage. That’s not the sexiest service, I would say. I will say what we’ve learned is that every service in and of itself has value.Some are going to drive a lot more revenue, like car rentals and luggage storage,” said Chesky during the earnings call.While luggage storage has proven unexpectedly popular, Chesky said the most widely used new service “by far” has been car rentals, with average rental durations exceeding the length of typical Airbnb stays. Both services have become revenue drivers, helping Airbnb compete more directly with hotels by offering conveniences travelers expect.Chesky emphasised that every added service increases the likelihood of guests booking through Airbnb, whether for homes or hotels. He said the company has a pipeline of dozens more services in development. Airbnb posted an earnings beat in Q3, with its stock rising about 10% in after-hours trading.Airbnb posted stronger-than-expected third-quarter results, with revenue growth exceeding analyst forecasts. The company’s earnings beat sent its stock up nearly 10% in after-hours trading, underscoring investor confidence in Airbnb’s strategy of expanding beyond rentals into guest services and experiences.In related news, recently Airbnb CEO revealed his plans on investing in New York. He said, “New York City has been part of our story since the earliest days of Airbnb. This building reflects our long-term commitment to the city and will be home to one of our largest employee hubs outside of San Francisco. We're excited to keep investing in the city and the people who make it extraordinary. ”Airbnb is also expanding into New York City for the first time after years of disputes over short-term rental rules. The move comes despite regulations, including 2022's Local Law 18 and a 30-day minimum stay requirement, that restricted its core rental business. Moreover, the company is buying a permanent home in Manhattan.
Article Summary: Airbnb CEO Brain Chesky revealed during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that the most popular new service wasn’t one of its AI-driven features, but rather a practical offering which is luggage storage. Airbnb introduced luggage storage in May through a partnership with Bounce, a global platform that helps travelers find secure places to store bags before check-in or after checkout.

Article Title: Michael Dell’s son Zach’s 3-year-old startup, currently valued at $13 billion wants to replace costly home generators in American homes with …
Article Text:
Base Power was founded in 2023 by Michael Dell's son Zach Dell

Zach Dell’s Base Power wants a battery in every backyard

Michael Dell’s son’s startups aims to offer alternatives to costly generators

Michael Dell’s son Zach Dell is betting big on home batteries. His three-year-old startup, Base Power, aims to replace expensive gas-powered home generators with battery systems that provide backup power during outages while also helping reduce electricity bills. Base says it wants to install its battery systems in neighborhoods across the US and eventually expand to Europe, as rising electricity demand driven by AI puts more pressure on power grids.The company is currently valued at $13 billion after raising $1 billion in a Series D funding round. The latest funding round was led by Ribbit Capital, Addition, Valor Equity Partners and JPMorgan Chase's Strategic Investment Group. Existing investors, including Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Lightspeed, Trust Ventures and CapitalG, also participated. While Michael Dell is not involved in Base Power's operations, Zach Dell said his father serves as a mentor.Base Power was founded in 2023 by Zach Dell and has grown rapidly. The Austin-based company has increased installations from one battery system a day to more than 100 daily and now serves over 30,000 customers."We want to bring Base to every neighborhood in America over time," Dell told Fortune. "The scale of the opportunity is just massive, and of course, we do have global ambitions. We think markets like the U.K., Germany, Australia, and potentially others are attractive as well."The company recently opened its first battery factory in Austin and is building a second, larger facility expected to be completed in 2027.Instead of selling traditional backup generators, Base installs battery systems that store electricity and can keep homes powered during outages for up to two or three days, depending on usage. Customers pay an installation fee starting at $695 and a monthly membership fee of $19, rather than buying a generator that can cost $15,000 or more.Unlike conventional standby generators that typically rely on natural gas or propane and operate only during outages, battery systems can also be used for everyday energy management by storing electricity when prices are lower and supplying power during peak demand."Our business model, which is very unique, is that we're really an infrastructure company," Dell said. "We own and operate the assets in the wholesale power markets. That's really where we make our money, not by trying to sell the consumer something at a really high-margin upfront cost."The company says its new battery stores 39.2 kilowatt-hours of electricity, more than many competing products. Base says its business is becoming more relevant as electricity demand rises because of AI data centres and increasing pressure on power grids."We're charging the batteries when prices on the grid are low, and we're discharging the batteries with demand when prices on the grid are high," Dell said.In just three years, the company has expanded from Texas into Illinois and plans to enter more US states next year. In some new markets, Base is offering battery installation for as little as $95 to attract more customers.
Article Summary: Base Power was founded in 2023 by Michael Dell's son Zach Dell. The Austin-based company has increased installations from one battery system a day to more than 100 daily and now serves over 30,000 customers. The company is currently valued at $13 billion after raising $1 billion in a Series D funding round.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg gave an update on ‘Meta's 4 am layoff email’ to employees during earnings call, shared expenses on …
Article Text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Mark Zuckerberg addressed ‘4 am layoff email’ during earnings call

Operating income impact

After layoff of 8,000 employees, Meta CEO spends $130 billion on AI

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently gave an update on ‘Meta's 4 am layoff email’ to employees during earnings call. In May this year, Meta fired roughly 8,000 employees. Thousands of employees across the globe received email from Meta leadership informing that their role has been eliminated. The email sent to impacted employees, obtained by Business Insider, gave details on severance, visas, and access to company systems. It said that employee access has been cut, but laid-off employees can check all details on Alumni portal, which they can access within an hour of losing system access. Meta reported Q2 revenue of $60.8 billion, up 28% year-over-year (27% on a constant currency basis). However, total expenses surged 55% to $42 billion, driven by higher employee compensation, infrastructure costs, legal-related charges, and third-party AI token expenses.Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg addressed the company’s widely discussed “4 AM layoff email” during the earnings call, noting that Q2 expenses included $1.2 billion in severance costs tied to the May 2026 headcount reduction. An additional $2.4 billion in legal charges also weighed on results. Meta ended the quarter with over 75,000 employees, down 3% from Q1, including approximately 8,000 impacted by the layoffs. The company expects most of those employees will no longer be counted in its headcount by the end of Q3.“We ended Q2 with over 75,000 employees, down 3% from Q1. This total includes approximately 8,000 employees impacted by the May 2026 headcount reduction. We expect the majority of impacted employees will no longer be captured in our headcount by the end of Q3 2026,” said Zuckerberg.Mark Zuckerberg also explained that growth in employee compensation was largely driven by technical hires, particularly in AI. Infrastructure costs rose due to higher depreciation, data center operations, and third-party cloud spending.Meta has been increasing investment in AI infrastructure while reshaping its workforce, reflecting a broader shift across the technology industry as companies redirect spending toward computing capacity, specialised talent and large-scale AI development.Meta’s GAAP operating income for the quarter was $18.8 billion, representing an 8% decline year-over-year and a 31% operating margin. Excluding severance and legal charges, operating income would have increased 9% compared to last year.“We expect the majority of impacted employees will no longer be captured in our headcount by the end of Q3 2026. Second quarter GAAP operating income was $18.8 billion, representing an 8% decline year-over-year and a 31% operating margin. Excluding the Q2 legal charges and severance expenses, our second quarter operating income would have increased 9% year-over-year,” added Zuckerberg.Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has a message for anyone anxious about AI taking their job: the technology is actually hiring. Speaking to the Wall Street Journal hours before Meta's June quarter earnings, Zuckerberg said that "all the work around AI has net created a lot of jobs because there's all this infrastructure that needs to get created," adding that fears of mass displacement haven't "played out the way that people feared it might. "It's a claim that invites an obvious question, because the company making it spent this year doing the opposite. Meta laid off 8,000 employees—about 10 per cent of its workforce—in May as part of an AI-first restructuring, reassigned another 7,000 to AI initiatives, and is on track to spend between $130 billion and $145 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, roughly double last year's outlay. Zuckerberg isn't wrong that AI is creating jobs. They just aren't the ones his own company eliminated.
Article Summary: Mark Zuckerberg addressed ‘4 am layoff email’ during earnings call. Meta reported Q2 revenue of $60.8 billion, up 28% year-over-year (27% on a constant currency basis) Total expenses surged 55% to $42 billion, driven by higher employee compensation.

Article Title: Microsoft's top AI boss has a message for engineers using GitHub Copilot: Your token spend is now being tracked
Article Text:
The company that sells AI is now rationing it internally

Nadella called himself a tokenmaxxer two months before the memo landed

Amazon, Adobe, Citi and Meta got here first

Microsoft has spent three years telling the world to use more AI. This week it told its own engineers to use it more carefully. In an internal email to his CoreAI organisation, executive vice president Jay Parikh wrote that "tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for" — and backed the line with policy. OpenAI's cheaper GPT-5.6 is now the default model for internal use, every Microsoft division has an AI token budget target, and employees can pull up a dashboard showing exactly what their own AI habit costs the company.The memo was first reported by 404 Media, which obtained it from a Microsoft employee who asked not to be named. The numbers inside are the eye-catching part. Microsoft's internal Copilot guidelines say many engineers spend anywhere from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand dollars a month on tokens. No hard cap figure has been shared yet, but the guidelines warn that further restrictions may follow as spending is monitored.Parikh framed the change as discipline, not distress. "As we accelerate our use of GitHub Copilot to deliver on our goals, we all need to be aware of how we consume tokens," he wrote, adding that Microsoft would manage token spend with the same discipline it applies to every other critical resource.He was careful to say this is not a retreat from being AI-first. "We are not optimizing for fewer tokens. We are optimizing for more impact per token. "The financial context supports him. Microsoft's latest earnings beat Wall Street on revenue, operating income and net income. This is not a company scrambling for cash. It is a company discovering that agentic coding tools consume tokens at a rate nobody budgeted for. Per-token prices have dropped roughly 98 percent since late 2022, yet enterprise AI bills have tripled, because an autonomous agent chewing through a repository burns through vastly more than an autocomplete suggestion ever did.The shift did not come out of nowhere. In June, at a live taping of the New York Times' Hard Fork podcast, Satya Nadella was asked how much tokenmaxxing happens inside Microsoft. "A lot," he said, cutting off the question. "I'm a tokenmaxxer too, it's addictive. But you have to step back when the novelty wears off to say, 'What is it that I'm trying to create?'" His advice then was to match the model to the task. Don't use frontier models for non-frontier problems.Microsoft had already been trimming. It cancelled most Claude Code licences in its Experiences and Devices group in May, pushing engineers to GitHub Copilot CLI before the fiscal year closed on June 30.Microsoft is arguably the last big name to formalise this. Amazon, Adobe, Atlassian and Citi have all introduced some form of AI throttling or spend visibility. Meta shut down "Claudeonomics," an internal leaderboard that had employees competing to burn tokens.Not everyone inside Redmond reads it as prudence. The employee who leaked the memo called it "the ultimate admission" that a company hosting AI infrastructure cannot afford its own AI products, and asked the obvious follow-up: how could the companies Microsoft sells to manage?Parikh's answer is in the memo itself. Keep using AI. Just know the bill has a name on it now, and it might be yours.
Article Summary: Microsoft has spent three years telling the world to use more AI. This week it told its own engineers to use it more carefully. In an internal email to his CoreAI organisation, executive vice president Jay Parikh wrote that "tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for"

Article Title: Two solar farms in Minnesota restored wildflowers, grasses and have population of bees, butterflies, wasps; scientists call it evidence of…
Article Text:
Two solar farms in Minnesota restored wildflowers, grasses and have population of bees, butterflies, wasps

The insect count that turned a Minnesota solar site into a research case study

Panel height quietly decides how much wildlife a solar farm can support

Native prairie habitat costs less than gravel across a solar farm's 25-year life

Most American solar farms still have no pollinator habitat at all

Two solar farms in Minnesota were built on retired agricultural land, and instead of the gravel or mown turf that usually goes under panels, the ground was seeded with native wildflowers and prairie grasses. Researchers from Argonne National Laboratory came back to the same test plots for five years and counted what flew and crawled past them. Insect abundance tripled. Native bees went up twentyfold.Bees, butterflies, wasps and hornets all turned up in greater numbers as the plantings matured. Lee Walston, the landscape ecologist who ran the fieldwork, builds his research around a plain question: "If you build it, will they come?" On land that used to grow row crops, the answer is yes—provided the right plants go into the soil.At an 18-acre site in Ramsey, north of Minneapolis, the method is unglamorous. Plastic flags mark the tracts, students walk the rows with clipboards, and everything spotted gets logged—a metallic green sweat bee here, a moth and two hoverflies there. Acoustic monitoring at the same site has picked up 73 bird species, drawn by the seeds and the insects. Some of them nest in the steel supports holding up the panels. The timing gives the numbers weight.Monarch butterflies are under federal review for endangered listing, and North American bird populations have fallen almost 30 percent since 1970.The Ramsey meadow exists because the panels sit higher than standard. A prairie restoration firm told ENGIE, the developer, that raising the arrays would let far more native species grow underneath without shading the glass. The extra steel and seed barely moved the project budget, and the site now needs a fraction of the mowing it otherwise would. Lower arrays leave landscapers with clover and a few grasses—better than gravel, nowhere near a prairie.The economics are less charming than the butterflies but more persuasive. Costed across 25 years, a native grass-and-forb mix works out to roughly $14,150 an acre, against $16,800 for standard turf grass and $25,000 for gravel. Maintenance drops sharply once the natives establish, usually after three or four years. There is a return at the farm gate too. A Nature Conservancy study in New Jersey found squash and blueberry yields rose 80 percent near pollinator habitat, with tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers and apples gaining 10 to 20 percent.Scale is where the story deflates. About 24,000 acres of US solar carry documented pollinator habitat, against roughly 600,000 acres of operating utility-scale sites, and meeting national energy targets could take close to 10 million acres of panels. At least 15 states run pollinator scorecards, but they largely rely on developer promises with no monitoring attached. One California project marketed as a pollinator solar farm pledged more than 200 native trees and shrubs along its perimeter; a UC Davis ecologist who walked the fence line found invasive grasses, yellow star thistle and the remains of a few plantings. The Xerces Society and an industry-funded research group are drafting a certification that would require 15 percent of a site's vegetated area to carry a diverse native mix.The Minnesota plots have settled the ecological question. What they cannot settle is whether the rest of the industry will pay for the taller steel.
Article Summary: Two solar farms in Minnesota restored wildflowers, grasses and have population of bees, butterflies, wasps and hornets. Most American solar farms still have no pollinator habitat at all. Costed across 25 years, a native grass-and-forb mix works out to roughly $14,150.

Article Title: SK Hynix commits $38 billion to two new chip fabs as AI memory demand refuses to cool
Article Text:
Image: SK Hynix

Yongin gets DRAM and HBM, Cheongju gets NAND

Memory prices are unlikely to soften before 2029

SK Hynix will spend 54 trillion Korean won, roughly $38.1 billion, on two new memory chip plants in South Korea, a bet that the AI data centre buildout still has years of runway left. The company's board approved the plan on Friday, splitting the money between a fabrication plant in Yongin, south of Seoul, and a second facility in Cheongju in the centre of the country.Neither one will produce a chip this decade's midpoint. The Cheongju fab breaks ground in February 2027 and opens its first cleanroom in December 2028. Yongin starts construction in July 2027, with its first cleanroom running by June 2029. So for anyone hoping this eases the memory crunch pushing up prices on phones, consoles and PCs, the answer is no, not for a while.The larger share, 35.2 trillion won, goes to the Yongin plant, internally called Y2. It will make DRAM, including the high-bandwidth memory that Nvidia's accelerators consume in enormous quantity. Y2 is the second of four fabs planned for the Yongin Semiconductor Cluster. The remaining 19.1 trillion won funds M17 in Cheongju, which will build NAND flash, a product SK Hynix says is seeing demand surge rapidly.Both sit inside a much bigger commitment announced last year: 600 trillion won for Yongin and 100 trillion won for Cheongju over time. SK Hynix pointed to Omdia forecasts showing DRAM and NAND demand growing 19% a year through 2030, and said the decision followed a thorough review of market demand.The timing matters because SK Hynix is under pressure at home. Samsung retook the top spot in DRAM market share during the second quarter, according to Counterpoint Research. "This has prompted SK Hynix to inject fresh capex to expand its footprint," Counterpoint's Neil Shah told CNBC, adding that it is built for 2029 and beyond rather than the current cycle.Shah expects supply from Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron and CXMT to expand significantly through 2028, but with demand outrunning planned capacity, he does not see prices easing before the end of that year. Micron has already walked away from consumer memory entirely to chase AI margins.
Article Summary: SK Hynix will spend 54 trillion Korean won, roughly $38.1 billion, on two new memory chip plants in South Korea. The company's board approved the plan on Friday, splitting the money between a fabrication plant in Yongin, south of Seoul, and a second facility in Cheongju.

Article Title: One of the world's popular jeans makers hacked: Read company’s full statement
Article Text:
Representative image

‘Corporate data extracted, operations unaffected’

Levi Strauss & Co. (the “Company”) recently detected that the Company experienced a cybersecurity incident in which an unauthorized third party gained access to Company files through social engineering techniques that enabled unauthorized access to three employees’ Company-issued computers. Following such detection, the Company initiated response protocols, implemented containment measures, launched an investigation, which remains ongoing and engaged the services of third-party cybersecurity experts.

Based on preliminary findings from the Company’s investigation, the Company believes that certain corporate information was accessed and exfiltrated as a result of the incident. As of the date of this filing, the Company believes that its rapid response efforts successfully contained and terminated the unauthorized access, and that no consumer data was impacted. The Company has not experienced any interruption in business operations as a result of the incident.

Based on information available as of the date of this filing, the Company does not believe the incident has had, or is reasonably likely to have, a material impact on the Company’s business strategy, operations, financial condition, or results of operations.

The Company has provided and will provide notifications to affected parties and applicable regulators as appropriate and in accordance with applicable law.

Part of a broader phone-based cyber campaign

Levi Strauss has disclosed that it fell victim to a recent cybersecurity incident after hackers gained access to its corporate network through a targeted social engineering attack on company personnel. The iconic jeans maker revealed the breach in a regulatory filing, stating that an unauthorised third party managed to breach its systems by tricking three employees into handing over access credentials.News agency Reuters reports that Levi Strauss joins a growing wave of global corporations facing aggressive cyber campaigns that aim to steal proprietary data and disrupt business operations.Following the intrusion, Levi Strauss initiated containment protocols and launched an internal investigation to determine the scope of the exposure, the company said. Preliminary findings indicate that attackers managed to view and extract certain internal corporate information. However, the company confirmed that its retail stores, e-commerce platforms, and daily supply chain operations experienced no disruptions.Executive leadership noted in the filing that the incident is not expected to have a material impact on the company's financial performance or operational strategy.The breach at Levi Strauss appears to be part of a larger, coordinated cyber campaign targeting major corporations across the US. Analysis of internet intelligence data reveals that ransom-seeking cybercriminals have increasingly relied on voice phishing, using phone calls to impersonate IT support or authority figures, to compromise corporate networks. Over the past five weeks alone, hackers created digital infrastructure traps targeting more than 200 companies, including prominent financial institutions and major brands.
Article Summary: The jeans maker revealed the breach in a regulatory filing. An unauthorised third party managed to breach its systems by tricking three employees into handing over access credentials. Levi Strauss joins a growing wave of global corporations facing aggressive cyber campaigns that aim to steal proprietary data and disrupt business operations.

Article Title: In 1962, a Wisconsin entrepreneur turned bus radio dispatch technology into America's first mobile pizza kitchen
Article Text:
Representative Image

How bus dispatch technology inspired mobile pizza kitchens

How pizza delivery changed in the US after World War II

Technical challenges limited the idea

"It'd be like Cirque du Soleil, basically,"

"Convenience is great, I get it,"

Expansion and eventual closure

Pizza once came from moving kitchens in America. In 1962, Wisconsin entrepreneur Dennis J. Sheahan adapted the radio dispatch technology he had developed for buses to launch Pizza on Wheels, a service that baked pizzas in specially equipped trucks while they drove to customers' homes. The idea turned bus communication systems into what became America's first mobile pizza kitchens.Customers placed orders through a central dispatcher, who used two-way radio to contact the nearest available truck. While the vehicle travelled to the delivery address, a chef inside prepared and baked the pizza so it could be served immediately after arrival. More than five decades before startups experimented with cooking pizzas in moving vehicles, Sheahan had already attempted the concept using mid-20th century technology.Sheahan, based in Reedsville, Wisconsin, had built radio dispatch systems for bus operators during the late 1950s. He later applied the same communication network to food delivery.Each Pizza on Wheels van was fitted with water tanks, sinks, refrigeration units, preparation counters and double-deck ovens. Customers called a central phone number, where a dispatcher received the order and then used radio equipment to identify the closest truck.Drivers then headed to the address while pizzas were assembled and baked inside the vehicle.The company advertised more than 25 topping combinations and promoted the service as delivering pizzas directly from the oven to customers' driveways.Pizza delivery in the US expanded rapidly after World War II as returning soldiers helped popularise the dish, while growing suburban communities and wider telephone use increased demand for home delivery.Although some pizzerias had begun offering delivery in the 1950s, orders often arrived after cooling in transit. Sheahan's mobile kitchen concept sought to solve that problem by preparing food en route rather than before delivery began.Pizza historian Carol Helstosky of the University of Denver told Popular Science that pizza has historically been suited to mobile selling, noting that pizza makers in Naples transported insulated boxes through the streets centuries before modern delivery services emerged.Despite its novelty, the concept presented practical difficulties. Refrigeration, food preparation, and oven operation inside moving vehicles posed challenges that pizza industry experts say would have been difficult to address with the technology available in the early 1960s."I've worked in the restaurant business my whole life and been a professional pizza consultant for about 15 years," Noel Brohner of Slow Rise Pizza told Popular Science. "I feel like I've heard it all." But, he admits, he'd never heard of this.Brohner also questioned how refrigeration, storage and food preparation could be managed safely inside a moving truck.Brohner said.Scott Wiener, founder of Scott's Pizza Tours, also said movement inside the vehicle would make preparing and baking pizzas considerably more difficult.Wiener stressed. "But you'll never get a quality pizza with this system."Despite the operational challenges, Pizza on Wheels expanded beyond its initial launch. After beginning with one truck in Kenosha in 1962, the company added three more vehicles in Madison the following year before expanding into Green Bay by 1964.Local newspaper advertisements from the mid-1960s also showed the company offering promotional deals and seeking franchise operators as it attempted to grow across the Midwest.By 1967, however, advertisements began appearing to sell Pizza on Wheels trucks. Some notices cited illness affecting a local operator, although the business gradually disappeared by the end of 1971.After more than 50 years had passed, the California-based company Zume tried its hand at this idea but abandoned this approach to pizza preparation in favour of other technologies before shutting down in 2023. This made “Pizza on Wheels” one of the earliest examples of such mobile-kitchen experimentation in American pizza delivery history.
Article Summary: Wisconsin entrepreneur Dennis J. Sheahan launched Pizza on Wheels in 1962. The idea turned bus communication systems into what became America's first mobile pizza kitchens. Customers placed orders through a central dispatcher, who used two-way radio to contact the nearest available truck. While the vehicle travelled to the delivery address, a chef inside prepared and baked the pizza so it could be served immediately.

Article Title: Michael Dell's son Zach Dell aims to install a Base Power home battery system in every backyard in America; and follows what is called Costco model
Article Text:
"We want to bring Base to every neighbourhood in America over time."

Zach Dell's Base Power to replace high upfront battery costs with a membership model

“Our business model, which is very unique, is that we're really an infrastructure company. We own and operate the assets in the wholesale power markets. That's really where we make our money, not by trying to sell the consumer something at a really high-margin upfront cost,”

Customer base and manufacturing expansion

Batteries designed for homes and the power grid

"This battery is designed to be a grid resource. It's bigger, it installs faster, it switches over cleaner, it's more powerful, it has more duration,”

Michael Dell's son is expanding its battery business. Zach Dell, the co-founder of the home battery company Base Power, says he wants to install a battery system in neighbourhoods across the US. In an interview with Fortune, he said:The company follows what Dell describes as a Costco model, offering low upfront installation costs and a monthly membership instead of selling high-priced battery systems.The expansion comes as Base Power announced a $1 billion Series D funding round, valuing the company at $13 billion, up from $4 billion in less than a year. Alongside its US expansion plans, Zach Dell said the company also has ambitions to enter markets including the UK, Germany and Australia, with its business model centred on low upfront installation costs and monthly membership fees rather than large one-time equipment purchases.Founded in 2023, Base provides electricity services alongside home battery systems that act as backup power during outages. Instead of selling customers a battery system costing around $15,000 or more, the company charges an installation fee of up to $695 and a monthly membership fee of $19.Dell described the approach as similar to the Costco model, in which recurring memberships, rather than high product margins, support the business.Dell said.According to the company, the batteries also return electricity to the grid when demand is high, which it says can help lower customers' overall electricity costs.Base said it has grown from installing one battery system per day to more than 100 daily, serving over 30,000 customers. Earlier this year, the company opened its first battery manufacturing facility, Base Factory 1, in Austin, while a second, larger factory is expected to be completed in 2027.The company initially launched in Texas and has since expanded into Illinois. Dell said Base plans to enter additional US states next year by either operating in deregulated electricity markets or partnering with monopoly utilities.The Series D funding round was co-led by Ribbit Capital, Addition, Valor Equity Partners and JPMorgan Chase's Strategic Investment Group. Existing investors, including Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Lightspeed, Trust Ventures, and CapitalG, also participated.Before opening its own manufacturing facility, Base relied on third-party battery systems. The company now produces batteries designed specifically for residential backup power and grid support rather than electric vehicle charging.Dell said.Base currently offers one- and two-battery systems. According to Dell, the company's latest battery stores 39.2 kilowatt-hours of electricity, allowing homes to continue receiving power during outages that last up to two or three days, depending on usage. Dell said the batteries are charged when electricity prices are low and supply power back to the grid when demand and prices increase.To support expansion in Illinois, Base has also introduced promotional installation pricing for some customers, reducing the installation charge from the standard $695 to as low as $95 in selected cases. Dell said the company expects to continue adjusting pricing as it enters additional markets.
Article Summary: Zach Dell's Base Power to replace high upfront battery costs with a membership model. Base Power announced a $1 billion Series D funding round, valuing the company at $13 billion. Alongside its US expansion plans, the company also has ambitions to enter markets including the UK, Germany and Australia.

Article Title: In September 2025, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman outlined a clear red line for AI, said: AI must be shut down immediately if it ever gains …
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman

‘AI’s four fatal capabilities’

“So those are the four criteria: Recursive self-improvement, setting its own goals, acquiring its own resources, and acting autonomously,

Nuclear-style regulation is not optional

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has outlined a firm “red line” for artificial intelligence (AI) safety, warning that if any AI system displays four specific autonomous capabilities simultaneously, it must be shut down immediately to prevent catastrophic risks. Suleyman cautioned that an AI model operating with these unrestricted capabilities could become so powerful over the next five to ten years that stopping it would require military-grade intervention.In a podcast with Trevor Noah , South African comedian and writer, in September last year, the tech executive said that to prevent such scenarios advanced frontier models must be subjected to strict auditing and oversight similar to the regulations governing critical national infrastructure like nuclear power.According to Suleyman, an AI system crosses a dangerous threshold when it combines four distinct autonomous traits. The first is recursive self-improvement, which is the ability for an AI model to rewrite, modify and optimise its own underlying source code without human input.The second is autonomous goal-setting wherein a system establishes its own objectives independent of programmer instructions. Next is the ability of autonomous action to execute decisions and interact with digital or physical systems without human authorisation.The fourth and final is the capability to independently acquire financial, computational or material resources to support its own operations.Suleyman emphasised that while individual capabilities are being researched across the industry, allowing all four to converge in a single system creates an unmanageable security threat.” Microsoft AI CEO said.Comparing the risks to high-consequence industries, Suleyman argued that developing superintelligent AI cannot remain an unregulated private enterprise.“Just like you can’t just go off and say, ‘I've got a billion dollars. I’m going to go build a nuclear power plant'... it’s a restricted activity because of the one-to-many impact it can have,” Suleyman said, urging industry leaders and governments to embrace formal regulatory frameworks.He added that tech companies and governments must collaborate on strict capability auditing before advanced models are deployed.
Article Summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has outlined a firm ‘red line’ for artificial intelligence (AI) safety. He warned that if any AI system displays four specific autonomous capabilities simultaneously, it must be shut down immediately. Sulyman cautioned that an AI model operating with these unrestricted capabilities could become so powerful over the next five to ten years that stopping it would require military-grade intervention.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda Gates: When a woman can step into her full power, it’s better for her, her children, her household, her community, and her country
Article Text:
Melinda French Gates

What Melinda French Gates said about empowering women

Why Melinda Gates ' quote matters

Melinda French Gates has spent decades speaking about the importance of giving women greater opportunities and economic power. Her words on women reaching their full potential offer today’s quote of the day: “When a woman can step into her full power, it’s better for her, her children, her household, her community, and her country. ” French Gates made the remark while speaking to more than 400 people at the Denver Center for the Performing Arts on April 22. She was being honoured by the University of Denver’s Josef Korbel School of Global and Public Affairs for her work in global health, gender equity and women’s economic empowerment.The quote reflects a central idea behind much of French Gates’ philanthropic work — that helping women gain access to opportunities, resources and decision-making power can have an impact that extends beyond the individual.Melinda French Gates has frequently emphasised that barriers that limit women’s participation in education, employment and leadership need to be removed for sustained economic growth and social progress. Gender equality has therefore been a common theme in her speeches and advocacy activities.Melinda French Gates has been involved in philanthropy for more than 25 years. She previously co-chaired the Gates Foundation before leaving the organisation in 2024.She also founded Pivotal in 2015, an organisation focused on advancing women and young people.During her conversation with Josef Korbel School dean Frederick “Fritz” Mayer, French Gates spoke about lessons she learned from her years in philanthropy. She explained that programmes intended to solve major problems may fail to achieve their full impact when women are not considered. She pointed to drought-resistant seeds in Africa as an example. Such seeds could help farmers deal with difficult climate conditions, but their impact would be limited if women farmers could not access the merchants selling them.“[I learned that] if we didn’t focus on gender, we were basically missing half the equation,” French Gates said.The quote highlights how empowering women can create wider economic and social benefits. French Gates' argument is that when a woman has the resources and opportunities to reach her potential, the benefits can extend to her children, family, local community and eventually the wider country.Her work through Pivotal follows a similar approach. The organisation invests in underrepresented entrepreneurs and supports efforts around issues including paid family leave and increasing women's participation in public office.Melinda French Gates also stressed that making a difference does not always require large amounts of money. People can contribute their skills, knowledge and time to causes in their communities.“There are many issues in your own community that can use your services, whether that’s your intellect, your time, the way you do finances, or marketing,” she said.She added, “One person does make a difference in the life of someone else; it doesn’t always have to be big.”
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates made the remark while speaking to more than 400 people at the Denver Center for the Performing Arts on April 22. She was being honoured for her work in global health, gender equity and women’s economic empowerment. The quote highlights how empowering women can create wider economic and social benefits.
